questions.q: What's the difference between fabula and syuzhet?
choices: Fabula is fiction, syuzhet is fact
Fabula is the events in chronological order; syuzhet is how they're presented
Fabula is the hero, syuzhet the villain
questions.explain: The Russian Formalists' distinction between what happened and how it's told.

questions.q: A film opens on a man lying dead, then cuts to 'Two weeks earlier'. What is this in Genette's terms?
questions.explain: After the opening, the telling jumps back: an analepsis, or flashback.

questions.q: 'Every Sunday the family walked to the river.' What kind of frequency is this?
questions.explain: Told once, happened many times. It lets a writer describe a pattern without inventing one day.

questions.q: A film tells the same crime from four witnesses' perspectives. Which frequency is this?
questions.explain: One event, told several times, as in Rashomon.

questions.q: A novel's narrator speaks in the third person but shows only what one character perceives. What has been separated?
choices: Who speaks and who sees: narration and focalization
questions.explain: Genette distinguished the narrator's voice from the focalizer whose perception the telling follows.

questions.q: In Chatman's terms, what happens if you cut a kernel?
choices: The logic of the story breaks, because kernels are its branching points
questions.explain: Satellites can be cut and the story survives; kernels can't.

questions.q: Why does this lesson matter so much to journalists?
choices: They can invent events to fit the order
They can't change the events, only the telling: order, speed and perspective
questions.explain: Reporters find the fabula and write the syuzhet; arranging it honestly is part of the ethics.

questions.q: What's the main criticism Culler and Herrnstein Smith made of the story/discourse split?
choices: There may be no fixed set of events underneath the tellings; sometimes the telling seems to produce the event
It puts the climax in the middle
questions.explain: They questioned whether a stable story always exists prior to, and independent of, its versions.

ideas: The events in the order they happened and the order in which they're told are two different things, and the art lies in the gap.
Telling once something that happened many times lets a writer describe a pattern instead of a single day.
Who tells a story and whose eyes we see it through are separate questions.
Some events are branching points that can't be cut; others only fill in and can go.
